extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of 19th-century American theatre and literature; readers of biography/history
extracted.subtask_description: Expository/biographical chapter describing the career, public honors, speeches, and critical reception of the 19th-century actor Edwin Forrest, with illustrative anecdotes and contemporary remarks. Focuses on qualities admired in actors, playwrights, orators, and the cultural role of press and nationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a distinguished actor
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor should combine 'an uncommon energy of character and peculiar personal aptitudes' adapted to 'hold the mirror up to nature' and to identify the stage with the classic drama; be a 'prompt, uniform, and liberal patron of his art'; cultivate personal exertion, study, and example; and by domestic life 'disarm' reproaches against the profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual evidence: speeches praise Forrest for making 'Shakspeare... ours', for devotion to the profession, for generosity to fellow artists, and for having 'personal exertion, study, and example' that promote the art. Delivery and manner are singled out as part of excellence (see 'delivery was natural, forcible, and unaffected'). The passage also celebrates actors who produce 'illusion's perfect triumphs'—where acting makes verse and sculpture seem inadequate—suggesting illusion-making and persuasive embodiment as key markers of acting success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic writing quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong dramatic work is 'fine, spirited, stirring', 'full of noble sentiments', and 'clothed in striking language'; early works that bear 'the unmistakable impress of rich and fruitful soil' indicate vigorous mind and promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: the 'Jack Cade' play is praised for spirit, noble sentiments, and striking language; 'Conrad of Naples' is described as showing a vigorous and searching mind. The narrator also notes essayist qualities—'energy and brilliance of style, the justness and solidity of his ideas, and the comprehensive range of his information'—as indicators of literary merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for successful oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful public speaking combines heartfelt convictions and rhetorical vigor ('fervid rhetorical sentences' and 'picturesque vigor') with delivery qualities (natural, forcible, unaffected), and must suit the tastes of the audience to elicit strong approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fourth of July oration is described as 'extraordinarily successful' largely because its style and temper matched its audience; the same orator's banquet speech was noted for natural, forcible, and unaffected delivery. Audience response (extravagant admiration, applause, tears) and wide dissemination (printed in journals, pamphlets) are used as measures of success, though the text also cautions that popular reception can overestimate literary/philosophic value from a 'sober judge' perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality (local rootedness) as a literary virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's nationality—rooting writing in native soil and local feeling—is a positive quality: 'Let our authors... strike their roots into their native soil' and cultivate a partiality for what is our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from Ingersoll: patriotic attachment in literature (nationality) provides distinctiveness and strength; comparing to Walter Scott, removing local prepossessions would weaken an author. The passage frames 'nationality' as desirable even if excessive, claiming it helps authors flourish and connect with their native audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and responsibility of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is characterized as 'the source and safeguard of social order, freedom, and refinement' and has a duty to encourage talent and promote appreciation and reward in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers at the banquet assert the press should support and encourage high order talents, promote their appreciation, and feel responsibility toward society. The press's recognition and recording of an actor's career is presented as an important public function and measure of worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: The formative power of encouragement and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely encouragement, prophecy, and patronage can reveal and foster latent talent—'a word in season... prophecy oftentimes shapes the event'—and a single supportive act or shout at the start can enable long-term success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the anecdote of the boy under nitrous oxide whose tragic declamation elicited a benefactor's encouragement (the future mayor), which is credited with helping shape Forrest's career. The text uses this to argue for the importance of early, generous support (public applause, hospitable gestures, mentorship) as evaluative context for later achievement.
